The early life stages of Platichthys stellatus are characterized by small size at key developmental transitions. Newly hatched yolk-sac larvae, emerging at a length of approximately 0.2 cm , depend entirely on endogenous yolk reserves. The duration of the egg stage is highly temperature-dependent; at 10.5 °C [T = 10.5 °C], eclosion occurs after about 4.6 days , whereas at a warmer 12.5 °C [T = 12.5 °C], development accelerates and hatching is observed after approximately 2.8 days . This thermal sensitivity during embryogenesis has profound implications for larval survival and recruitment success in the variable coastal environments the species inhabits. The size at the moment of exit from the chorion, known as length at hatch, is a useful comparative metric across flatfishes.

Following the lecithotrophic yolk-sac phase, the onset of exogenous feeding marks a critical trophic switch. The total duration spent as a non-feeding larva, the time since hatch at birth, is approximately 2.8 days  at 12.5 °C [T = 12.5 °C]. Upon complete yolk-sac resorption, the pelagic larva must successfully capture its first prey to avoid starvation. This period of early larval life is a major bottleneck for population replenishment. As the larva grows, it undergoes pronounced morphological transformation, culminating in the larval-juvenile transition. The individual reaches metamorphosis at a length of approximately 1.05 cm , a stage defined by the migration of the left eye towards the ocular side and the onset of benthic settlement. This body plan reorientation is one of the most dramatic developmental events in teleost biology.

Sexual maturation in Starry flounder exhibits a clear dimorphism, with females reaching puberty at a larger size and later age than males. Under thermal conditions around 4 °C [T = around 4 °C], females attain puberty after roughly 3 years [tp = roughly 3 years], corresponding to a length at puberty of approximately 29 cm [Lp = approximately 29 cm]. In contrast, males mature faster and at a smaller size; the time since birth at puberty for males is around 2.5 years [tp = around 2.5 years], occurring at a length at puberty of approximately 27.5 cm [Lp = approximately 27.5 cm]. at a temperature of 4 °C [T = 4 °C]This protandrous pattern of maturation is common among pleuronectiforms and is thought to maximize reproductive output given the species' size-related fecundity. Following puberty, individuals continue to grow slowly over many years.

Growth continues throughout life, albeit at a decelerating rate, leading to substantial differences between the sexes in maximum size. The ultimate total length for females is approximately 91 cm [Li = approximately 91 cm], a size that corresponds to an impressive ultimate wet weight of approximately 13,000 grams [Wwi = approximately 13,000 grams]. These figures are derived from field surveys of the largest documented individuals, with the weight-length relationship closely following a cube-law allometry. In contrast, length at birth is a mere 0.35 cm [Lb = 0.35 cm], reflecting the modest dimensions of the newly emerged embryo. The corresponding wet weight at birth is very small, on the order of 0.00045 grams [Wwb = 0.00045 grams], based on an egg diameter of about 0.95 mm. This roughly six order-of-magnitude increase in body mass over the lifetime underscores the prodigious growth capacity of this species.

The maximum recorded lifespan for Platichthys stellatus is 24 years [am = 24 years] at a sustained temperature of 4 °C [T = 4 °C], a relatively long duration that highlights a slow-paced life history compared to many other boreal teleosts. At the same thermal regime, the species achieves a high reproductive output; females produce approximately 300,000 offspring per spawning event [N_R_i = approximately 300,000 offspring per spawning event] and are capable of approximately one spawning event per year [F_R_i = approximately one spawning event per year], a combination that yields a daily fecundity of around 822 eggs per day. Such an elevated reproductive investment, coupled with a long reproductive lifespan, allows females to offset high larval mortality and maintain stable populations in the face of variable environmental conditions. These life-history attributes position the Starry flounder as a resilient inhabitant of cold, productive North Pacific waters.
